problem: The notation contradicts the figure. The text defines "switch Sij connects input i to output j", but the figure labels the nine devices S1 to S9 row by row: S1, S2, S3 are the three switches feeding output A. A student applying the Sij rule would read S2 as "input 2 to output 2", not "input b to output A", so the worked state (S2, S6, S7) cannot be decoded from the stated definition.
fix: Drop the Sij form and define the flat numbering: "The nine switches are numbered row by row. S1, S2, S3 connect inputs a, b, c to output A; S4, S5, S6 connect a, b, c to output B; S7, S8, S9 connect a, b, c to output C." Then S2, S6, S7 give A = b, B = c, C = a, matching the figure.

problem: "Two outputs may share an input in some states, but many schemes avoid it to keep input currents balanced" misleads. States in which outputs share an input cannot be avoided in practice; the zero states connect all three outputs to one input and are used in every space-vector scheme. It is the choice of states, not avoidance, that shapes the input current.
fix: "In many states two or three outputs share one input phase. The zero states connect all three outputs to a single input. The mix of states chosen sets the input current waveform and its balance."

problem: "The input voltage triangle" is not defined anywhere and is not a triangle in this context. A student cannot see where the √3/2 comes from.
fix: "The limit comes from the envelope of the three input phase voltages. At any instant the output must lie between the largest and the smallest of va, vb, vc. That envelope has peak Vin,peak and its lowest peak is Vin,peak × cos 30° = (√3/2)Vin,peak, so the biggest clean sine output has peak (√3/2) times the input peak."
